Introduction

This chapter provides criteria for evaluating perma-nent impairment of the hematopoietic system. The hematopoietic system, including the bone marrow, lymph nodes, and spleen, produces a heterogeneous population of blood-circulating cells (eg, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets) and a complex family of proteins critical for blood clotting and immune defenses. Cells from this system also pro-duce proteins that affect daily physiologic responses (eg, granulocyte stimulating factors and granulocyte-macrophage stimulating factors) and respond to many pathologic stimuli (eg, by producing tumor necrosis factor and interleukins). Because the hema-topoietic system supports other cells or organs of the body, identifiable defects in these organs due to hematologic disease are assigned impairment ratings directly; the hematologic rating does not generally include the physiologic effects of hematologic dis-ease or cancer on the function of other end-organs. For example, very severe anemia can reduce oxygen delivery to the point where the individual suffers a myocardial infarction. The impairment ratings

for both the anemia and the myocardial infarction would be rated separately and then combined. Age and comorbid conditions further complicate the determination of impairment. Most of the products of the hematopoietic system also include remarkable compensatory biologic mechanisms.

Clinical alterations can be hereditary or acquired. Because of functional adaptation of the young, hereditary defects manifested in childhood are com-monly modest in degree of impairment. With age, alterations become more significant and functional impairment more evident. Abnormalities can be quantitative—production of too many cells (ie, leu-kemia or polycythemia) or too few cells (ie, anemia or thrombocytopenia)—or they can be qualitative, with production of a defective protein (ie, factor V Leiden or prothrombin 20210A) resulting in an increased propensity for thrombosis.

The new hematopoietic chapter in the Sixth Edition of the Guides differs significantly from the hema-tology chapter in the Fifth Edition. There are new tables for use in rating leukemia and lymphoma, metastatic disease, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and bleeding disorders. There are also expanded sections on human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and thrombotic disorders, as well as an overall revi-sion of tables to comply with the format described in Chapter 1. As with other chapters, the goal is to provide tools that enable evaluators to more accu-rately and consistently choose an impairment per-centage that reflects the unique characteristics of the disease process rated. This has led to an increased emphasis on combining ratings to reflect the impact of hematologic or oncologic disease on myelogenous elements rather than implicitly incorporating these effects in the initial rating, as well as to an increased emphasis on explicit use of functional scales in the ratings for HIV and cancer.

The class ratings for some of the processes consid-ered reflect factors that have an impact on the abil-ity of the individual with that disease to perform Activities of Daily Living (ADLs); no separate functional scale is used for these. On the other hand, there is a wide variation in the ability of patients with HIV, leukemias, lymphoma, or metastatic dis-ease to maintain ADLs, which is to a large extent dependent on their ability to tolerate medications or chemotherapy. The use of a functional scale is consequently a component of the rating for these diseases. Although the Fifth Edition used a generic functional scale, there are 2 scales commonly used in oncology and for the classification of impairment due to HIV disease, the Karnofsky Performance

Status Scale1 and the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status Scale2 (ECOG-PSS). It would appear logical to use these scales rather than the generic scale; they are used as part of the basis for rating the leukemias, metastatic disease, and HIV infection. Both are described in this chapter, with guidelines provided for their use.

Another significant change in this chapter is with regard to the ratings used for each class. The model described in Chapter 1 of the Guides is used, with a key factor driving the impairment class assign-ment and the other factors determining at what grade (percentage) the rating falls in a particular class. The ratings for all classes, especially class 4, have been decreased, as once one moves to higher levels of impairment, there is inevitably involvement of other organ systems or other hematologic processes. These should be identified, rated, and combined with the hematology-oncology impairment rating. The Burden of Treatment Compliance, as discussed in Section 9.1c, contributes further to the impairment rating.

The differences in clinical implications regarding movement from one class to another are large. The difference in the choices for ratings in classes 3 and 4 as opposed to lower classes reflects the difference between having signs and symptoms that are gener-ally controlled by treatment versus those that are uncontrolled by treatment. As hematologic and onco-logic diseases are systemic in their manifestations, uncontrolled disease is highly significant clinically and warrants the high levels of impairment seen in these classes.

9.1 Principles of Assessment

Before using the information in this chapter, the Guides user should become familiar with Chapters 1 and 2 and the Glossary. Chapters 1 and 2 discuss the Guides’ purpose, applications, and methods for per-forming and reporting impairment evaluations. The Glossary provides definitions of common terms used by many specialties in impairment evaluation.

9.1a Interpretation of Symptoms and Signs

Some impairment classes refer to symptoms that limit the ability to perform daily activities. When this information is subjective and open to misinter-pretation, it should not serve as the sole criterion on which decisions about impairment are made. Rather, the examiner should obtain objective data about the extent of the limitations and integrate those findings

with the subjective data to estimate the degree of permanent impairment.

Impairment percentages may reflect severity of symptoms, physical and laboratory findings, and estimated functional limitations resulting from hematologic abnormality. The Karnofsky Performance Status Scale has 10 different categories for patients and is widely used to describe the func-tional ramifications of both oncologic disease and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS; Table 9-1). The ECOG-PSS is also used widely to classify functional deficits as related to oncologic disease, it refers to the Karnofsky scores when assigning func-tional grades, and assigns patients into functional classes ranging from grade 0 to grade 4 (Table 9-2). As the use of 5 grades in the ECOG-PSS is con-sistent with the general structure of the grids used for impairment ratings, it will be used explicitly for the functional classification of patients with AIDS and oncologic disease, and as one of the implicit criteria for assessing the functional impact of hema-tologic disease. In general, the class structure used in impairment ratings for specific disease processes will follow that used in the ECOG-PSS. Activities of daily living are listed in Table 1-1 and the Glossary.

9.1c Burden of Treatment Compliance (BOTC)

While treatment for hematologic and oncologic disease often leads to a diminution of symptoms and/or signs of disease, side effects (both local and systemic) can be considerable. Part of this Burden of Treatment Compliance is reflected in the impairment ratings given for the disease process; however, there is widespread variation between patients with regard to the need for medications, procedures, or treat-ments such as corticosteroids, anticoagulant therapy, transfusions, hemophoresis, and both oral and intra-venous chemotherapy. Table 9-3 is to be used to assign additional impairment percentage points to reflect the BOTC for hematologic disease. A sum-mary of rules for assigning impairment percentages for BOTC is given in Table 9-3.

Although in prior editions of the Guides an additional 10% impairment rating could be given to patients who are controlling signs or symptoms of their disease with anticoagulant ther-apy, a rating of 5% would seem more appropriate. An impairment rating of 10% is applied to individu-als who have had a bone marrow transplant.

The long-term use of corticosteroids can be associated with ratable entities such as osteoporosis, avascular necrosis, diabetes mellitus, and Cushing’s disease; however, other effects are not easily rated but impose some degree of impairment. To the extent that these are deemed present and not captured by the rating for any organ system or systems, the evaluator is permitted to add up to 3% additional impairment. As there is a great deal of variation in the severity and degree of side effects from steroids, the rationale for assigning additional impairment percentages must be documented. The use of chelation therapy or immuno-suppressive drugs may also result in significant side effects in susceptible individuals. In these cases an additional 1% to 3% impairment to reflect the BOTC can also be added to the final rating.

Oral forms of chemotherapy also vary widely in the degree to which they are tolerated. Although there is no impairment rating that will ordinarily be given for use of oral chemotherapy in addition to that for the disease being rated, the evaluator can add a dis-cretionary rating of 1% to 5% for BOTC but must justify the rationale for doing so (eg, menopausal symptoms in a woman receiving tamoxifen as jus-tification for a 3% additional rating). The 5% rating

would be reserved for situations in which the che-motherapy leads to systemic effects that have a clear impact on the ability to perform ADLs. Intravenous chemotherapy is more complex. While the functional impact of medication intolerance or side effects will be reflected by the ECOG-PSS or Karnofsky Scale, additional impairment develops when patients must receive multiple cycles of chemotherapy over a relatively short period (as frequently as weekly), especially if multiple agents are employed. The evaluator is encouraged to defer rating those diseases that will require only limited courses of chemo-therapy to induce remission, as it is preferable to wait until Maximum Medical Improvement (MMI) has been reached. Some conditions will require repeated cycles of chemotherapy; there are also situ-ations when a rating must be done as a consequence of other conditions (eg, a musculoskeletal injury sustained at work) regardless of whether the patient has reached MMI with regard to the management of other conditions. Under these circumstances, the evaluator can add discretionary additional impair-ment percentages of 1% for each cycle of chemo-therapy, up to a maximum of 6%, to reflect the effect of chemotherapy on ADLs, with the total additional impairment equal to the number of cycles of chemo-therapy provided during the 6-month period before the rating. The same concept is also applicable to patients receiving regular radiotherapy to control signs and symptoms of disease, although in this case the additional impairment will be 1% per week of radiotherapy during the prior 6 months.

Lastly, the need for transfusions, phlebotomy, or aphoresis on a regular basis has an impact on the ability to sustain ADLs, at least intermittently. As there is wide variation in the degree to which patients with a given diagnosis will require these interventions, the impairment ratings provided in the tables in this chapter do not include the addi-tional impairment that results from their use. When applicable the evaluator is to assign an additional 1% impairment per unit of blood transfused each month, 1% per episode of therapeutic phlebotomy per month, and 3% impairment per episode of aphoresis per month.

9.1d Methodology for Determining the Grade in an Impairment Class

This chapter employs impairment grids to use in determining the appropriate impairment class (class) and severity grade (grade) within a class for the condition or conditions being rated at Maximum Medical Improvement (MMI). As was stated in chap-ter 1, the decision regarding which factor is the pri-mary determinant of impairment (key factor) will be

clearly stated in each organ system impairment grid. The examiner will use this key factor to determine the appropriate class with the middle grade (integer) in that class as the initial (default) rating (Refer to Table 9-4).

The examiner will then use non-key factors to assign grades for factors other than that considered “key,” with it being impossible to move upward or down-ward between classes based on these non-key factors. The number of potential grades for each impairment class varies based on the number of relevant factors. When there are 2 non-key factors, there are generally 5 impairment grades per class; the presence of only one relevant factor other than the key factor reduces the number of possible grades to 3 per class.

If the examiner determines that the other factors affecting the rating are in the same class that had been used for the key factor rating, the final rating will generally stay in the middle of that class. On the other hand, if the classes chosen are higher or lower than that used for the baseline impairment rat-ing, the level will be moved to the right or to the left (to a higher or lower value) to reflect the numerical discrepancy. For example, if the key factor places the initial rating in class 3, grade C and there are 2 non-key factors (leading to a total of 5 possible grades) that are in class 1 and class 4, respectively, the first factor would move the grade down 2 levels to grade A and the second would move it back up 1 level to grade B. However, if both non-key factors were class 1, the rating could not go any lower than class 3, grade A, the lowest value for the class. An exception to this rule may occur when the key factor is in the highest impairment class for the disorder, as non-key factors falling in the same class can be used to adjust the impairment rating upward to the highest grade within the class rather than keep it at the middle

level. Specific tables will indicate if a rating schema other than this is used.

The impairment criteria generally used in this chap-ter on the hematopoietic system may include the his-tory, physical findings, and objective test results. The assignment of a key factor and relative importance of the criteria will vary according to each regional disorder.

9.2 Anemia

The functional effects of chronic anemia depend on the degree of the cardiovascular system’s compensa-tory response. Regardless of the pathogenesis of the anemia, impairment is related to the heart’s inability to deliver adequate oxygen to tissues. To compen-sate for the anemia, the heart increases cardiac out-put by acceleration of heart rate and also increases oxygen extraction from the tissues (ie, increases arteriovenous difference). Therefore, a person with a mild anemia—a hemoglobin level of approximately 100 g/L (10 g/dL)—and a normal cardiovascular system receives a lower impairment rating than a person with underlying dysfunction of the cardio-vascular system.

Symptoms of anemia include shortness of breath or chest pain on exertion, dizziness, throbbing headaches, and fatigue. The speed at which anemia develops at any hemoglobin level correlates to the complexity of symptoms. Greater degrees of anemia may be associated with lack of stamina, fatigue on exertion, fatigue at rest, and dyspnea at rest. Thus, no specific concentrations of hemoglobin determine impairment. Anemia impairment is measured by the limitations of cardiovascular response and may be

Given the wide variation in symptoms seen at a particular level of hemoglobin, it appears most appropriate to consider the history as the key factor in rating anemia. The functional ramifications of anemia are included in the rating and, hence, are not considered separately.

Many forms of anemia are reversible with specific therapy. Anemias resulting from decreased red blood cell production due to nutrient deficit (eg, iron- deficiency anemia, megaloblastic anemia secondary to folic acid, and vitamin B12 deficiency) are correct-able with specific nutrient therapy.

A permanent impairment may develop from sequelae of the anemia. Often this is due to decreased oxygen to a vital organ such as the heart, leading to a myocardial infarction. In megaloblastic anemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency, significant neurologic deficits caused by demyelinization (par-ticularly of the posterolateral spinal tracts) may occur and result in permanent neurologic impair-ment. Folic acid deficiency during pregnancy may result in lifelong impairment of the newborn with varying degrees of neural tube defects. In some circumstances of hypoproliferative anemia resulting from chronic renal failure, the anemia is correct-able with exogenous erythropoietin, even though the renal failure is irreversible. Similarly, many forms of anemia due to increased and, particularly, acquired red blood cell destruction (ie, hemolytic anemias) are reversible with therapy and therefore do not result in permanent impairment.

Persistent hemolytic anemia may cause a degree of impairment that is related to the severity of the ane-mia. This impairment consideration also applies to aplastic or refractory anemia caused by defective bone marrow function. Persistent refractory anemia may cause impairment regardless of the cause; the degree of impairment is related to the severity of the anemia, need for transfusion, and impact on the ability to perform ADLs. Additional organ system impairment due to anemia can be combined using the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix. If bone marrow trans-plantation has been performed and was unsuccessful, an additional 10% impairment is assigned in addition to the impairment assigned for the primary disorder, which will often be considerable.

The benefits of red blood cell transfusion normally last less than 3 weeks. In individuals with hemolytic ane-mia caused by serum factors, and in some who have had many transfusions, the survival rate of transfused cells is shortened and transfusions must be repeated as often as every few days. Impairment increases as

hemolysis becomes more severe. An additional impair-ment percentage of 1% is given to reflect the BOTC for each unit of blood transfused per month. As noted pre-viously, since the degree to which individuals require transfusions is often independent of their disease or the severity of symptoms, it is appropriate to add the BOTC for transfusions to the baseline impairment rat-ing in those situations when it is used.

In congenital hemolytic anemias, particularly those related to altered hemoglobin synthesis (eg, hemo-globinopathies and thalassemias), tissue impairment beyond the hematopoietic system results in perma-nent impairment.3 Sickle cell anemia is commonly associated with severe, painful vaso-occlusive crisis that can result in functional impairment of varying degrees.4 These vascular occlusive lesions result in end-organ damage to the bones, heart, kidneys, and liver, compounding the degree of impairment. These disorders can also require chronic exchange transfu-sion every few weeks.

CLASS 1 1% to 5% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 9-2: ANEMIA WITH RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS

Subject: 48-year-old woman.

History: More than 10-year history of rheumatoid arthritis, managed with acetylsalicylic acid, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and intermittent corticosteroid therapy.

Current Symptoms: Occasional fatigue, stiffness in hands, and difficulty performing ADLs.

Physical Exam: Joint deformities in both hands con-sistent with rheumatoid arthritis.

Clinical Studies: Hemoglobin: 102 g/L (10.2 g/dL). Hematocrit: 31. Mean corpuscular volume: 79. Serum ferritin: 250 μg/L (250 ng/mL). Remainder of labora-tory findings normal except for rheumatoid factor.

Diagnosis: Anemia with rheumatoid arthritis.

Impairment Rating: Class 1, grade B impairment of 3% due her fatigue (mild symptom). Her hemoglo-bin of 102 g/L (10.2 g/dL) is also class 1, so her rat-ing remains 3%. Combine with an impairment rating for joint changes from rheumatoid arthritis.

Comment: Unlike the rheumatoid arthritis, the ane-mia is mild. In some people with rheumatoid arthri-tis or chronic inflammatory lesions, iron-deficiency anemia develops due to medication and gastrointes-tinal blood loss. This woman’s normal serum ferritin level does not necessarily rule this out, as ferritin levels are increased in the context of inflammation, which may elevate a low ferritin level due to iron deficiency to normal levels. Her anemia is that seen in the anemia of chronic disease.

CLASS 2 7% to 15% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 9-3: AUTOIMMUNE HEMOLYTIC ANEMIA

Subject: 59-year-old man.

History: Found to be anemic 2 years after a lung infection.

Current Symptoms: Fatigue; takes naps several days per week; doesn’t do vigorous work such as shoveling snow or prolonged yard work.

Physical Exam: Normal; no palpable liver or spleen.

Clinical Studies: Hemoglobin: 95 g/L (9.5 g/dL). Hematocrit: 29. Serologic evidence of cold agglu-tinins. Low-grade hemolysis with agglutination on peripheral smear; elevated mean corpuscular volume and reticulocyte count, positive direct Coombs’ test.

Diagnosis: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia of the cold antibody IgM type.

Impairment Rating: 11% impairment of the whole person. His symptoms put him in class 2, grade B (11%). His hemoglobin level is also consistent with this class, so he remains at that level.

Comment: Chronicity of anemia is established; there is no specific therapy. Anemia limits perfor-mance of daily activities. Exposure to colds or viral illnesses carries a risk of abrupt, enhanced red blood cell destruction with a further anemia. In some indi-viduals, particularly in older age groups, a malig-nant lymphoma may develop. Regular follow-up is recommended.

CLASS 3 25% to 45% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 9-4: SICKLE CELL ANEMIA

Subject: 22-year-old woman.

History: Sickle cell anemia since birth. Repeated pain crises. Hemoglobin 85 to 95 g/L (8.5 to 9.5 g/dL) for the last 5 years, without adequate response to hydroxyurea. Pain crises occur 4 to 6 times per year and usually require hospitalization, narcotics, and sometimes transfusion (approximately 4 times a year). Performance of daily activities limited since moderate physical work can provoke a pain crisis. She receives folic acid and narcotics as needed.

Current Symptoms: Slight fatigue; takes naps when not having a pain crisis. Usually off work several times per year for several days per occurrence due to pain crisis episodes.

Physical Exam: Sickle cell habitus.

Clinical Studies: Hemoglobin: 82 g/L (8.2 g/dL). Hemoglobin electrophoresis review: confirms sickle cell hemoglobin (SS) with normal fetal and A2 hemoglobin.

Diagnosis: Sickle cell anemia.

Impairment Rating: 25% impairment of the whole person. Her history is consistent with class 3, grade B (35%) but her relatively good hemoglobin level and the need for only infrequent transfusions moves her down 1 grade to a 25% impairment rating.

Comment: Increased risk of other, potential sequelae—avascular necrosis of the femoral heads, cardiomyopathy, renal failure, and so on—requires careful monitoring and, if present, will lead to the assignment of additional impairment percentages. Transfusions provide transient support and are mainly used for crisis intervention.

EXAMPLE 9-5: CHRONIC ANEMIA WITH MYELODYSPLASTIC SYNDROME

Subject: 48-year-old woman.

History: Fatigue, decreased appetite, and limited energy 1 year ago led to recognition of a progressive anemia. Erythropoietin has not increased red blood cell values. Requires transfusions of 1 to 3 U of packed red blood cells every 4 to 5 weeks.

Current Symptoms: Fatigue; decreased energy; needs to rest and take an afternoon nap daily. Can perform light ADLs with help. Feels better for 7 to 10 days after transfusions and then declines in function.

Physical Exam: Signs of anemia; otherwise normal.

Clinical Studies: Bone marrow: myelodysplasia with excess blasts. Hemoglobin: 69 g/L (6.9 g/dL) but often lower, although usually not lower than 60 g/L (6 g/dL).

Diagnosis: Chronic anemia with myelodysplastic syndrome.

BOTC: Average transfusion requirements of 2 U per month leads to the assignment of an additional 2% impairment.

Impairment Rating: 37% impairment of the whole person. Her history is consistent with class 3, grade B (35%) and transfusion requirements, so she stays at grade B (35%), to which 2% for BOTC is added.

Comment: Condition is likely to progress in terms of the severity of the anemia, with an increase in the frequency of transfusions required since isoimmu-nization is an inevitable sequela. If her hemoglobin levels were often under 60 g/L (6 g/dL) necessitating more frequent transfusions, she would move to class

4. Individual is at increased risk of transformation to acute leukemia and iron overload due to transfusion requirements, although this could be managed with deferasirox (Exjade). Some unusual forms of myelo-dysplasiamay respond to treatment with lenalido-mide (Revlimid) or 5-azacytidine.

EXAMPLE 9-6: APLASTIC ANEMIA

Subject: 32-year-old woman.

History: Severe aplastic anemia diagnosed 4 years ago. Failed immunosuppressive agents and bone marrow transplantation. Now requires 3 U of packed red blood cells every 4 weeks.

Current Symptoms: Fatigue, especially before transfusions. Very limited exercise tolerance; able to walk for only 5 to 10 minutes before fatigue and shortness of breath occur.

Physical Exam: Signs of anemia.

Clinical Studies: Hemoglobin: 67 g/L (6.7 g/dL) but average hemoglobin level usually below 60 g/L (6 g/dL).

Diagnosis: Aplastic anemia.

BOTC: 3% additional impairment is assigned for her transfusions.

Impairment Rating: 58% impairment of the whole person. Her symptoms and transfusion requirements put her in class 3 (35%), which is adjusted to the highest grade in this class (45%) based on her hemo-globin level. To this is added 10% for failed bone marrow transplantation and 3% for BOTC, yielding a total rating of 58%.

Comment: Chronic, severe anemia with contin-ued, significant transfusion needs; ongoing risks of hemochromatosis and comorbid problems likely, which may lead to the assignment of additional impairment.5

CLASS 4 55% to 75% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 9-7: ANEMIA

Subject: 36-year-old woman.

History: 2-year history of cerebrovascular accident, with a severe anemia associated with iron deficiency. Budd-Chiari syndrome developed 4 months ago, for which she has been placed on a regimen of warfarin sodium (Coumadin).

Current Symptoms: Weakness and fatigue; pale skin.

Physical Exam: Pallor; residual left-sided weakness. Pulse: 100 beats per minute.

Clinical Studies: Hemoglobin: 65 g/L (6.5 g/dL). White blood cell count: 2.5 × 109/L (2.5 × 103/μL). Platelets: 80 × 109/L (80 × 103/μL).

Diagnosis: Aplastic anemia, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, and Budd-Chiari syndrome.

BOTC: She received a rating of 5% due to the use of warfarin.

Impairment Rating: 60% hematologic impairment of the whole person. Her history puts her in class 4 and starts at 65% (grade B), her hemoglobin level of 65 g/L (6.5 g/dL), in class 3, moves her to a lower impairment grade (55%) for this class and the use of warfarin leads to the addition of 5% for a total rat-ing of 60%. 9.3 Myeloproliferative Disorders, including Polycythemia, Myelofibrosis, and Essential Thrombocytosis

Polycythemia vera is manifested by hematocrit values above 52% in men and 49% in women, and by red blood cell volumes above 0.036 L/kg (36 mL/kg) in men and 0.032 L/kg (32 mL/kg) in

women. Other associated signs and symptoms are normal arterial oxygen tension, an enlarged spleen, slight elevation of the white blood cell and platelet counts, and increased leukocyte alkaline phos-phatase. Diagnostic criteria might include analysis for a mutation in JAK2. An increase in red blood cell numbers (polycythemia) can be due to car-diopulmonary disease, smoking, or inappropriate secretion of erythropoietin. If the primary cause of erythrocytosis can be treated and the erythrocytosis corrected, there should be no permanent impair-ment. Phlebotomy to normal hematocrit levels might minimize the symptoms of all forms of polycythe-mia. Polycythemia can lead to other organ system impairments, such as cerebrovascular or cardiovas-cular occlusions.

Myelofibrosis (bone marrow fibrosis) may also occur in individuals with polycythemia. Although some individuals remain relatively asymptomatic for several years, others experience fatigue, weak-ness, weight loss, perspiration, low-grade fever, and an enlarged spleen. Currently, no therapy exists that consistently relieves the symptoms of myelofibro-sis. Transfusions may be needed for severe anemia. Exogenous erythropoietin increases red blood cell production in some people.

Essential thrombocytosis is a disorder of unknown etiology manifested clinically by the overproduc-tion of platelets without a definable cause. The dis-ease can occur at any age, and patients affected by this disorder are largely asymptomatic and do not experience either hemorrhage or thrombosis. Anemia rarely develops; a mild leukocytosis can occur at times. Symptomatic treatment with salicylates may help those patients in whom neurologic symptoms such as headache do develop. If platelet reduction is deemed necessary, interferon-α or anagrelide can reduce platelet count, but in the absence of symp-toms no treatment is required.

9.3a Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Polycythemia, Myelofibrosis, or Essential Thrombocytosis

Polycythemia can produce end-organ damage to car-diovascular or cerebrovascular areas due to vascular occlusion. Vascular obstruction of the portal venous system similarly can produce end-organ injury to the liver. There is no specific rating given for the polycy-themia, with the impairment rating based on the end-organ involved and the degree of injury, to which is added any impairment rating given for phlebotomy (if used to control disease) or chemotherapy. There is also no rating given for essential thrombocytosis,

although in those rare occasions when symptoms develop the rating should be based on the organ sys-tem affected or on the degree to which hemorrhagic or thrombotic events occur.

The criteria for diagnosis of myelofibrosis, of pri-mary (idiopathic) or secondary (postpolycythemic) etiology, include progressive anemia with red blood cell changes of anisocytosis and poikilocytosis, a shift to the left of the granulocytic white blood cell series, and, often, nucleated red blood cells in the peripheral blood. Bone marrow biopsy indicates fibrosis with dilated sinusoids and clustering of megakaryocytes. The level of impairment due to myelofibrosis is reflected by the level of impairment due to the anemia and/or neutropenia. The primary deficiency is rated first and combined with the impairment rating due to deficiencies in other cell lines. (See Tables 9-5 through 9-7.)

9.4 White Blood Cell Diseases or Abnormalities

The primary function of white blood cells (leu-kocytes) is providing protection against invad-ing microorganisms, foreign proteins, and other materials. Three separate white blood cell “fami-lies”—granulocytes, lymphocytes, and monocytes-macrophages—interact to provide this protection. Each white blood cell family has a fixed tissue com-ponent that provides the renewal or precursor pool and also functions at fixed sites, including the bone marrow, spleen, and lymph nodes. Abnormalities in white blood cells are expressed as both numbers and alterations in function.

9.4a Granulocytes

Granulocytes protect against infection through the phagocytosis of invading organisms. They function primarily at the site of tissue invasion; the observa-tion or enumeration of granulocytes in the circulation indicates inflammation or infection. Granulocytes have a brief half-life of approximately 6 hours. The granulocyte precursor pool is in the bone marrow, where a very large production capacity exists.

Abnormal granulocyte function is usually congeni-tal, although acquired functional abnormalities may result from drug use or toxin exposure. Frequent infection is an indicator of defective granulocyte function; infection may vary from localized, self-limited infections such as furunculosis to life- threatening infections such as recurring septicemia. Type, frequency, and severity of the recurring infections are the basis for evaluating impairment. An affected individual will have a reasonably consistent infection pattern that facili-tates treatment and enables a judgment concerning prognosis.

Two different forms of quantitative granulocyte abnormalities are granulocytopenia and leukemia. Granulocytopenia is characterized by a significant decrease in the total number of granulocytes in the blood. Severe infections due to low numbers are uncommon, unless the granulocyte count is less than 0.50 × 109/L. Irreversible chronic neutropenia with counts below 0.50 × 109/L is associated with a substantially increased risk of infection; the infec-tion defines impairment. Table 9-6 is used for rating impairment due to neutropenia. Objective findings are the key factor.

9.4b Lymphocytes

Lymphocytes provide humoral and cellular defense mechanisms. Circulating lymphocytes originate in lymphoid tissues: the bone marrow, spleen, lymph nodes, and thymus. Lymphocytes circulate between the blood and the tissues. Lymphocyte cells have heterogeneous functions. They produce cytokines, which is a usually a normal function. There are no data to support cytokine testing for any causation impairment rating or to assess disability.

Of the 2 major subgroups, the “T,” or thymus-derived lymphocytes, are primarily responsible for protection from viral and other infections and for cellular immunity, and are involved in delayed hypersensitivity reactions and transplant rejection. The “B,” or bone marrow-derived lymphocytes, are primarily responsible for humoral immunity related to the production of immunoglobulins. Subtypes of both T and B lymphocytes have distinct functions and abnormalities that produce distinct clinical syndromes.

Lymphocytes can be abnormal in function and/or number, often leading to recurrent infections. Individuals with Hodgkin’s disease or connective tissue diseases and those who have been exposed to ionizing radiation all have acquired functional defects. Some “autoimmune” diseases may be a result of functionally altered or numerically pre-dominant subsets of lymphocytes. Impairment rat-ings due to abnormal numbers of lymphocytes, as with lymphopenia, are based on the severity of the condition, as indicated by recurrent infection, and a limited ability to perform ADLs.

The best documentation of defective lymphocyte function or numbers is to determine failure of end functions like generalized immunoglobulin defi-ciency or delayed hypersensitivity reaction failure. Lymphocyte abnormalities are associated with 3 forms of neoplastic transformation: (1) leukemias (including chronic lymphatic leukemia, acute lymphatic leukemia, and hairy cell leukemia)6; (2) lymphomas (including Hodgkin’s disease, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, and mycosis fungoides); and (3) multiple myeloma and macroglobulinemia.

Chronic lymphatic leukemia, hairy cell leukemia, and some low-grade lymphomas may be relatively indolent, require no initial therapy unless severe and irreversible, and constitute no impairment for several

years. However, since complete cure can be obtained with chemotherapy for hairy cell leukemia, defini-tive treatment should be initiated once the diagnosis is made. Multiple myeloma and macroglobulinemia may be asymptomatic initially, manifested only by certain laboratory abnormalities, and constitute no impairment. All leukemias, regardless of cell line derivation, will be rated using Table 9-7. History is key factor. Lymphomas behave more like solid tumors than leukemias and should be rated using Table 9-13, combined with any rating for the effect of the lymphoma on a specific organ system.

9.4c Impairment from Leukemias

Leukemias are classified as acute or chronic. The 4 major classifications are: acute myelogenous leuke-mia (AML), chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML), acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL), and chronic lymphocytic (lymphoid) leukemia (CLL). They result in impaired function of the individual and limited life expectancy, even with currently available therapy. Impairment is based on symptoms, physi-cal findings, the requirement for and frequency of therapy, and the ability to carry out ADLs. Use Table 9-7 for both myeloid and lymphocytic leukemias.

Symptoms resulting from the lymphocytic and myeloid leukemias are due to the leukemia, its effects on the number or function of other types of blood cells, or its effects on other organ systems. Leukocytosis, leukopenia, anemia, or thrombocyto-penia are the main hematologic consequence. There is also a relative loss of function of the cell type causing the leukemia, because while the cell count may be high, many of the cells are immature blast forms and therefore nonfunctional. There also are occasions when some of the leukemias lead to eryth-rocytosis or thrombocytosis. In all of the leukemias one should first rate the disease (based on Table 9-7) and then rate the hematologic manifestations of disease or the effect of disease on other organ sys-tems. These should be combined to arrive at a final rating using the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix, which will lead to the final rating for the leukemia or lymphoma.

In AML and ALL, there are large quantities of immature, and hence poorly functional, cells, leading to the development of bacterial, fungal, or viral infections; symptomatic anemia; or bleeding. Patients with CLL are often fully functional dur-ing early-stage disease, because while the cell count may be high, the function of other cell lines is nor-mal. 9.4d Myelodysplastic Syndromes

Myelodysplasia of hematopoietic precursors is more frequently recognized after age 50 years. It occurs as a primary (idiopathic) or secondary form, com-monly after exposure to a wide variety of industrial chemicals or after cytoreductive chemotherapy or radiation therapy for neoplastic disease. Causative factors include several drugs, particularly topoisom-erase inhibitors and platinum derivatives. The prin-cipal primary or secondary hematopoietic changes are defective and decreased cellular proliferation and production. Cell line (red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets) involvement and progres-sion are variable. (For more information, refer to Tables 9-5, 9-6, and 9-9 for rating impairment due to anemia, granulocytopenia, and thrombocytopenia.) Eventually, all cell lines become involved; at least one-third of patients progress to a leukemic transfor-mation. For unknown reasons, patients with myelo-dysplasia have more constitutional symptoms than expected for peripheral hematologic value levels. Myelodysplasia impairment evaluation is based on the degree of individual component alteration and on its effects on other organ systems.

9.4e Impairment from Human Immunodeficiency Virus Infection

Infection with HIV creates a progressive and ulti-mately fatal disease process with a complex course

and widely variable degrees of functional impairment. This virus can directly destroy CD4 T lymphocytes, resulting in impairment of the normal immune response against infection and neoplastic processes. The risk of developing opportunistic infection is, in general, inversely related to the absolute CD4 count.7,8

Impairment with HIV infection is caused by single- or multiple-organ system involvement from primary HIV infection or the opportunistic infection or neoplastic process from immunologic dysfunction. Essentially, every organ system can be affected, including hematologic, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, neurologic, dermatologic, and renal. Several systems are often simultaneously affected, adding to the complexity of impairment determination.

Acute retroviral syndrome may develop early in HIV infection; symptoms include fever, fatigue, pharyngi-tis, rash, myalgia, and arthralgia. Quantitative HIV RNA measurements also indicate the extent of HIV infection. Early stages are characterized by a CD4 count greater than 0.50 × 109/L (500 cells/μL); indi-viduals are often asymptomatic but may have lymph-adenopathy, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and dermatologic conditions. Intermediate stages have CD4 counts of 0.20 × 109/L to 0.50 ×109/L (200 to 500 cells/μL); antiretroviral therapy is often initi-ated to prolong this stage of disease. Individuals may have few or no symptoms or may experience consti-tutional symptoms, diarrhea, herpes simplex infec-tion, oral or vaginal candidiasis, upper respiratory tract infection, sinusitis, or common bacterial infec-tion. Advanced stages, often defined by CD4 counts less than 0.20 × 109/L (200 cells/μL), are associated with an increased incidence of opportunistic infec-tion and meet the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) definition for AIDS. At low CD4 levels, there is increased incidence of complica-tions, including Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia; Toxoplasma gondii encephalitis; tuberculosis; cryp-tosporidiosis; salmonellosis; esophageal candidiasis; neoplasms, including Kaposi’s sarcoma, lymphoma, and cervical cancer; and neurologic dysfunction, such as mononeuritis multiplex, peripheral neuropa-thies, cranial nerve palsies, and myelitis. At CD4 levels below 0.10 × 109/L (100 cells/μL), the follow-ing are more common: HIV-associated dementia, wasting syndromes, progressive multifocal leukoen-cephalopathy, cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis, dis-seminated Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC), cryptococcal meningitis, disseminated coccidiomy-cosis, histoplasmosis, and invasive aspergillosis.

The degree of symptomatic involvement and the course of illness in individuals with the same CD4 cell-defined stages vary significantly. Functional

impairment can also develop from toxicity responses to antiretroviral treatments, including reverse tran-scriptase inhibitors; viral protease enzyme inhibi-tors; and antibacterial, antiviral, antifungal, and antineoplastic therapies. Determine total impair-ment only after careful assessment of each of the potentially affected organ systems. Also consider the nature and severity of the primary or second-ary infections or neoplastic processes. Do not rate HIV disease using any of the standard hematologic tables. Instead, use Table 9-8. Objective findings are key factor. Although the degree of impairment from HIV approaches 100% in those patients with end-stage disease, this is due both to the HIV infec-tion itself and involvement of other organ systems. Consequently, the top rating for class 4 is 80%, with the understanding that this will be adjusted upward once impairment in other organ systems is combined with that from HIV.

9.4f Monocytes-Macrophages

The monocyte-macrophage family ingests foreign proteins, removes cellular debris, particulates mate-rial, and modulates immune responses. This functional unit of circulating monocytes and fixed macrophages, “histiocytes,” is structurally associated with endothelial cells and fibroblasts in the reticuloendothelial system. This system is recognized primarily by the phagocytic capacity of monocytes and macrophages.

Knowledge about functional defects in the monocyte-macrophage system is limited. The degree of impair-ment can be associated with the nature, type, and extent of infection. Lipid storage disease is another abnormality in which macrophages become reposi-tories for lipids, and cellular and organ hyperplasia occurs in the spleen, lymph nodes, and bone marrow. Marrow involvement can produce progressive and massive bone abnormalities and fractures; impairment focuses on the degree of orthopedic deficit.

Neurologic involvement also occurs in some severe forms of lipid storage disease. Enzyme replacement therapy is now available for Gaucher’s disease, one of the most common types of lipid storage disease. This therapy is effective at reversing most abnor-malities except for neurologic deficit. Impairment depends on the nature of the lipid, rate of deposition, and primarily affected organs.

Neoplastic transformation occurs primarily as acute monocytic leukemia, a relatively rare form of leu-kemia. The exact cell of origin is not clear, but the condition behaves as a form of chronic neoplastic transformation. In general, ratings for disease of monocytes or macrophages are achieved by rating the effects of disease on other aspects of the hema-topoietic system and/or on other organ systems com-bined with use of the table for leukemia (Table 9-7).

9.4g The Spleen and Splenectomy

The spleen is a large lymphoid organ that plays an important role in innate and adaptive immune responses. As a consequence of splenectomy, some functional abnormalities may develop. These include impaired clearance of certain encapsulated bacteria, such as the pneumococcus. Occasionally, overwhelm-ing infections develop after splenectomy. This occurs in fewer than 2% of people from whom the organ has been removed and is confined mostly to children or during the first 2 years after the operation. The incidence has been greatly reduced by prophylactic administration of the polyvalent pneumococcal vac-cine. Splenectomy leads to some subtle, albeit clini-cally silent, morphologic abnormalities of red blood cells and a transient elevation of the platelet count. Splenectomized individuals are not at an increased

risk of viral infections. If an individual experiences repeated infections after splenectomy, an impairment rating of 5% should be assigned and added to the hematologic rating. Otherwise the impairment rating is 0. Splenomegaly of greater than 5 cm below costal margin is uncomfortable and usually affects ability to eat by causing early satiety. This leads to assignment of an impairment rating of 5%, which is added to the hematologic impairment, if present.

9.5 Hemorrhagic and Platelet Disorders

Hemorrhagic disorders include coagulation disorders and platelet disorders.

Hemorrhagic disorders are either congenital or acquired. In most hereditary disorders, the basic hemostatic defect remains unchanged throughout the individual’s life. People with hereditary blood

coagulation disorders may require prophylactic therapy to help them perform activities they might otherwise avoid because of the threat of trauma. To control bleeding, many patients may require frequent home treatment, which interferes with daily activity. Impairment ratings vary depending on the frequency of treatment and on the extent of interference with normal activity. (See Tables 9-1 and 9-2.)

Von Willebrand’s disease is frequently mild; bleed-ing occurs only after trauma or surgery. It does not affect function significantly enough to warrant an impairment rating. However, some individuals meet criteria for a significant impairment rating because of recurrent bleeding.9-12

Severe inherited bleeding disorders may cause com-plications such as joint dysfunction from recurrent hemorrhaging. Impairment due to this complica-tion is evaluated with criteria found in Chapter 15, The Upper Extremities, and Chapter 16, The Lower Extremities. If several organ systems are impaired, the whole person impairment percentages are com-bined (see Combined Values Chart in the Appendix).

9.5a Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Platelet Disorders

Thrombocytopenia is not rated for impairment unless it is severe, affects function, and is irrevers-ible by steroids, splenectomy, or other therapeutic regimens. Qualitative platelet defects rarely meet criteria for impairment rating unless there is seri-ous bleeding, which also may occur in some rare congenital disorders. There is wide variation in the degree to which individuals with a given platelet count will sustain hemorrhagic events.

Autoimmune thrombocytopenia may require long-term immunosuppressive therapy, which can lead to dysfunction of several organ systems and can hamper daily activities. Complications are evaluated according to the criteria of the affected body system or organ and combined with the impairment percent-age for the appropriate blood platelet disorder (see the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix). The impairment criteria for platelet disorders are given in Table 9-9. History is key factor. The patient must also be rated for any impairment in other organ sys-tems that has resulted from hemorrhagic events.

9.5b Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Clotting Disorders

Congenital deficits in clotting are generally due to factor VIII or XIX deficiencies or von Willebrand’s disease. Factor levels determine the degree to which the former will be symptomatic, whereas the abso-lute degree of the deficiency is less important in von Willebrand’s disease. There are other hemorrhagic disorders as well; however, in all of them impairment is primarily caused by the frequency of hemorrhagic events. Any physiologic abnormalities that develop as a consequence of these events are to be rated separately and combined with the impairment from the hemorrhagic disorder.

Acquired blood-clotting defects are usually second-ary to severe underlying conditions. For example, individuals with severe liver disease may have impaired production of clotting factors leading to a hemorrhagic diathesis. Individuals may also develop antibodies against normal clotting factors as in acquired hemophilia. Individuals with venous or arterial thromboembolic disease who receive anti-coagulant therapy with a vitamin K antagonist (eg, warfarin sodium) need to be monitored chronically to ensure a therapeutic degree of anticoagulation. If these individuals become over anticoagulated, they may have a hemorrhagic consequence.

Hemophilia is typically divided into 3 categories based on the degree of factor deficiency. This cor-relates well with the frequency and risk of hem-orrhagic complications. Individuals with mild hemophilia (5% to 30% of normal) typically do not

bleed spontaneously but do need to be premedicated before surgery. They may respond to desmopressin (DDAVP), which will temporarily increase their factor VIII levels. Those individuals who do not respond to this medication and those with lower clotting factor levels (under 5%) require clotting fac-tor infusions, usually self-administered. These are sometimes given on a chronic basis to individuals with clotting factor levels under 1% as prophylaxis against bleeding. Individuals with hemophilia may develop antibodies against exogenously adminis-tered factor. This is a complication of therapy, which complicates the treatment of hemorrhagic events; these individuals are sometimes given chronic fac-tor or immunosuppressive therapy. There is also variation in the frequency of hemorrhagic events between individuals with similar levels of factor deficiency. Table 9-10 is used to rate impairment due to the hemophilias. History is key factor. Impairment resulting from hemarthroses is rated separately and combined with the impairment from the hemophilia.

9.6 Thrombotic Disorders

Thrombotic disorders involve arteries, veins, or both. Thrombosis may be either primary due to an inherited disorder or secondary due to acquired conditions. Whereas each risk factor may contribute to thrombosis, combined factors may lead to a greater risk.13

9.6a Inherited Thrombotic Disorders

Known defects include: proteins C, S, and anti-thrombin III deficiency; gene mutation associated with increased activity of a clotting factor (eg, factor V Leiden and prothrombin 20210A); and increased homocysteine levels due to cystathionine B-syn-thase deficiency (although homocysteine levels are also due to deficiencies of vitamin B12 or folate). Hyperhomocysteinemia is associated with athero-sclerosis and thrombosis of the arteries and some-times of the veins. Forty percent of individuals with thrombosis have 1 or more of the aforementioned abnormalities. Clinical indications of congenital thrombotic abnormality include family history; occurrence at an early age; recurrence; and occur-rence at unusual sites (eg, mesenteric, portal, splenic, renal, cerebral, or retinal veins).

9.6b Acquired Thrombotic Disorders

Acquired thrombotic conditions associated with venous thrombosis include antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (found in some patients with arterial throm-bosis), malignancy, use of certain estrogen-containing drugs, obesity, immobility, postoperative phase, multi-ple trauma, pregnancy, heart failure, use of indwelling venous catheters, sickle cell disease, inflamma-tory bowel disease, diabetes, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, and myeloproliferative disorders. The acute phase of venous thrombosis is usually treated with unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin, then oral anticoagulation for 3 to 6 months. Individuals with a greater risk of thrombosis require anticoagulation, either temporary (postsurgical) or lifelong (as prophylaxis for inherited thrombotic dis-order and recurrent thrombosis). Arterial thrombosis is treated according to the system involved. The length of time patients need to be treated with oral antico-agulation depends on a complex set of parameters, including the presence of reversible risk factors, his-tory of previous events, type of underlying thrombo-philia (if any), and clinical presentation.

Thrombotic disorder impairment results from systematic complications after thrombosis and anticoagulation regimen. It depends on the type, site, and extent of the organ involvement, as well

as the response and complications of anticoagula-tion. Arterial thrombi may produce ischemic heart disease, stroke, or intermittent claudication. Venous thrombosis often resolves with no aftereffects. If unresolved, postthrombosis syndrome may develop due to vein lumen narrowing and/or venous valve insufficiency, causing lower extremity edema, venous ulceration, venous thrombosis recurrence, and ambulation limitation.

9.6c Criteria for Rating Permanent Impairment due to Thrombotic Disorders

Impairment is evaluated based both on the throm-botic disorder itself and the impact of thromboses that have occurred on a particular affected body system. With regard to the former, regardless of the cause of the thrombotic abnormality, impairment is due to restrictions necessitated by the disorder itself (eg, avoidance of prolonged sitting, high temperatures with limited access to fluids, or strenuous activities), anticoagulation given for the disorder, or, rarely, from a continued tendency toward thrombosis despite adequate anticoagulant therapy. The tendency toward thrombosis depends on the nature and extent of the underlying thrombotic disease, as modulated by the use of oral contraceptives, certain types of estro-gens and other procoagulant medication as well as whether the affected individual smokes. There also appear to be other factors specific to the individual that have an impact on the risk of thrombosis; these have not yet been fully quantified. When a throm-bosis occurs due to a work-related event, the need for lifelong anticoagulation will reflect discovery of an underlying congenital problem that was previ-ously not identified (eg, a protein C or S deficiency). In these situations it is important to differentiate the impairment due to the congenital thrombotic abnormality from the impairment resulting from the effects of a given thrombotic event or events.

Individuals with a hypercoagulable state cannot be rated (ie, are not at MMI) until those conditions that warrant the use of anticoagulants have received an adequate trial of an appropriate agent. Some indi-viduals continue to have thrombotic events despite adequate anticoagulation; others cannot tolerate anticoagulation or refuse it. The rating is therefore based on the frequency of thrombotic events after MMI has been achieved; this is then adjusted to reflect the nature of the underlying hypercoagulable state. If the individual is receiving long-term anti-coagulant therapy for the thrombotic disorder with warfarin, low-molecular-weight heparin, or heparin, 5% is added to the impairment rating. This reflects the significant risk of bleeding that results from the

use of medications such as warfarin and the limita-tion of activities that results. Those receiving other forms of anticoagulation subsequent to surgical pro-cedures, such as cardiac stenting or neurologic con-ditions such as transient ischemic attacks or stroke, can receive up to 3% to reflect the BOTC from the use of these medications if there is strong evidence that their use has led to modification of significant ADLs (see Chapters 4, Cardiovascular System and 13, Central and Peripheral Nervous System).

If an individual cannot tolerate anticoagulant therapy or does not have severe enough disease to warrant its use, the degree of impairment depends on the likeli-hood of thrombosis. The most objective way to assign a severity grade is to use the nature and extent of the thrombotic disorder as a guide, since there is variation in the degree to which individuals with a given throm-botic disorder will become symptomatic. Impairment from the thrombotic disorder is to be given only if the affected individual has not been placed on a regimen of anticoagulant therapy. Whole person impairment from thrombotic disorders is listed in Table 9-12. Frequency of thrombotic events is key factor.

Any additional impairment from the thrombotic disor-der is based on the degree of injury to the end-organ, such as the lungs, heart, brain, kidney, and extremi-ties; from thrombosis; and on how the disorder affects the individual’s capacity to perform ADLs. Regardless of the system involved, the rating that results due to the sequelae of thrombotic disease should be com-bined with the impairment from the thrombotic disease itself (to which is added 5% for the use of anti-coagulants, if appropriate, before combining) using the Combined Values Chart in the Appendix.

The presence of metastatic disease materially alters the clinical presentation of a particular form of cancer, both through involvement of other organs and the burden caused by the systemic effects of the metastatic disease, any chemotherapy that may have been prescribed, and the functional ramifications of disease. Lymphoma is different pathologically from the leukemias as there can be more systemic signs and symptoms of disease. This is the rationale for combining these disorders. As once the rater has assigned an impairment rating that reflects local effects, the frequency of chemotherapeu-tic intervention and the functional impact of disease are the other indexes used to assess impairment, since they are surrogate markers for the remaining aspects of the disease process. No rating is automatically assigned for oral chemotherapy given prophylactically, although the examiner can give up to 5% impairment representing the BOTC on a discretionary basis. Likewise, no rating is given for a course of chemotherapy provided before a surgical procedure or until 2 weeks after a course of treatment has been provided. Criteria for rating perma-nent impairment due to lymphoma and metastatic disease is listed in Table 9-13. History is key factor.

CLASS 4 65% to 85% Impairment of the Whole Person

EXAMPLE 9-25: HODGKIN’S DISEASE

Subject: 28-year-old man.

History: Initial response to 2 cycles of ionizing radiation. Disease recurred, and he is now receiving 6 months of chemotherapy every 2 weeks for a total of 12 treatments. If the disease goes into complete remission, there is consideration of treatment with autologous bone marrow transplant. Patient gets average of 2 U of red blood cells per month.

Current Symptoms: Profound weakness due to anemia that temporarily responded to drug treatment and transfusions but has now recurred. Pruritus, chills, and fever. Still able to do basic ADLs.

Physical Exam: Lymphadenopathy below and above diaphragm.

Clinical Studies: Lymph nodes biopsy showed Hodgkin’s disease. Hemoglobin 79.0 g/L (7.9 g/dL) (as low as 75 g/L, or 7.5 g/dL, before transfusions).
